discovery: Optical lattice clocks reaching 10^-18 level precision and accuracy

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision metrology
motivation: Katori conceived the optical lattice clock and the 'magic wavelength' trap, which removes the light shift that had seemed to rule out confining atoms tightly without disturbing their clock transition. He and Ye turned this idea into clocks that interrogate thousands of neutral atoms at once. Ye's work on ultrastable lasers, frequency-comb-based comparisons and many-body control of strontium lattice clocks has taken stability and accuracy to the 10^-18 level and beyond. These clocks now measure the gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences, search for variations of fundamental constants and dark matter, and serve as the basis for redefining the SI second. This is precision measurement at its best: a dogma-breaking concept, carried through with outstanding experimental control, that has turned time into the most precisely measured quantity in physics and opened new tests of fundamental physics.
